column1: Algorithm|An executable sequence of steps for solving a task; a training algorithm produces a model rather than being that model.|Sorting orders by amount follows an algorithm.
Model|A representation that maps inputs to outputs. In machine learning, training adjusts its parameters using data.|A demand model estimates next week's sales.

Training|The process of adjusting model parameters using examples to learn patterns. Training performance alone does not establish generalization.|Learn demand patterns from past orders, then evaluate on a separate period.
Inference|Using an already trained model on an input to produce an output, normally without updating its parameters.|Drafting a reply to a new support ticket is inference.
Prediction|An estimate of an unknown outcome from input information and learned patterns; assess both error and its business consequences.|Overestimating demand can increase excess inventory.

Artificial intelligence (AI)|A field concerned with systems performing tasks such as perception, reasoning and decision making. Machine learning is one approach within AI.|Compare an intelligent assistant with a simple fixed approval rule.

Machine learning (ML)|Learning patterns from data rather than explicitly coding a rule for every case; evaluate against a defined task on unseen data.|Learn unusual transaction patterns from historical transactions.
Generative AI (GenAI)|AI that generates content such as text or images. Fluent output may still contain unsupported claims.|Check an interview summary against the original recording.
Structured data|Data organized with a defined schema or fields. A clear structure does not guarantee accurate values.|An order table has date, product and quantity fields.
Unstructured data|Information without the fixed field structure of a conventional table, such as prose, images and audio.|Transcribe a customer call before extracting the request.
Data quality|The fitness of data for its intended use, including accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness and relevance.|Investigate duplicate orders before comparing demand models.

Generalization and historical data|Generalization is useful performance on unseen cases; historical conditions may differ from deployment conditions.|Monitor a sales model after a new promotion changes demand.

Training, validation and test sets|Training fits parameters, validation supports development choices, and a held-out test estimates final performance. Leakage makes evaluation misleading.|Keep test-ticket answers out of training and evaluation inputs.

Shared AI vocabulary|Consistent definitions help teams distinguish models, algorithms, training and inference when making decisions.|Training completed does not mean deployment is operationally ready.

AI standards and management frameworks|ISO/IEC 23053 addresses frameworks for AI systems using ML; ISO/IEC 42001 addresses an organizational AI management system. Neither guarantees zero model errors.|Separate technical system design from management responsibilities.

Rules or AI|Prefer explicit rules for stable, well-defined conditions; assess AI for complex patterns, accounting for value, errors and maintenance.|A fixed expense threshold can use a deterministic rule.

AI agents and tools|An agent coordinates actions and tools toward a goal with some autonomy; permissions, supervision and failure handling require explicit design.|A refund agent needs an amount limit and escalation path.

Multi-agent orchestration|Coordinating roles, information exchange and execution among agents. More agents do not automatically improve outcomes.|Preserve sources and permissions when handing retrieved evidence to a drafting agent.

Drift and ongoing monitoring|Changes in inputs or relationships can reduce model performance; monitor quality, costs and feedback after deployment.|Investigate new customer language when complaint classification degrades.

Tool policies and shadow AI|Define approved, restricted, blocked and evaluated tools, their data boundaries and supported alternatives.|Tell employees which approved service can handle sensitive documents.
Prompt engineering|Design instructions with a goal, relevant context, constraints and output expectations; evaluate on representative tasks.|Ask for three summary points with supporting passages.

Tokens and context windows|Tokens are units processed by a model; the context window limits information available in a request, including input and output budgets.|Select relevant textbook passages instead of assuming every file fits.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)|Retrieve relevant authorized information and provide it as context for generation. Retrieval and answers still require verification.|Check a policy assistant's source version and access permissions.
Fine-tuning|Further training that adjusts model parameters for a task or behavior, distinct from adding information to a prompt.|Separate a style adaptation need from a need for current policy facts.

From business problems to use cases|Specify the affected people, workflow and observable problem before mapping AI capabilities to desired outcomes.|Reduce time spent finding authorized policies while preserving response quality.

Build, buy or partner|Compare internal capabilities, delivery time, budget, supplier constraints, integration, maintenance and exit costs.|A team without operations capability must consider support requirements.

Project prioritization|Rank initiatives by value, feasibility, sustainability and strategic fit; define evidence and conditions for stopping or scaling.|Validate data availability before committing to a high-return proposal.

When not to use AI|Choose alternatives when rules or process improvements solve the problem more reliably or errors outweigh benefits.|Improve document organization before commissioning a new AI system.
Migration and business continuity|Plan dependencies, staged migration, fallback procedures and ownership to maintain essential operations.|Keep an approved fallback route during a system transition.

Tangible and intangible benefits|Distinguish measurable financial or operational benefits from less direct effects such as trust or experience; state measurement assumptions.|Measure time saved and assess customer experience separately.
Business baseline|A measured reference for the existing process, needed for a meaningful before-and-after comparison.|Record current handling time and error rates before a pilot.
Benefits and ROI|ROI compares net benefit with investment over a defined period; include ongoing costs and explicit assumptions.|If benefits are 150 and costs are 100, ROI is (150-100)/100 = 50%.
Leading indicators|Early measures signal likely progress but are not proof of realized business value.|Usage can inform adoption monitoring without proving improved profit.

Cost planning and optimization|Account for development, data, integration, inference, monitoring, support and maintenance over the lifecycle.|Include review effort and ongoing operating costs in the budget.
Competitive landscape|Assess industry conditions, competitors and customer expectations before choosing an AI investment.|Identify a customer need rather than copying a competitor's demo.
Business model transformation|AI can change how value is created, delivered and captured, beyond automating an existing task.|Consider whether a personalized service changes the revenue model.

Sustainable advantage|Durable advantage depends on capabilities, workflows, data and learning that competitors cannot easily reproduce.|A widely available model alone is unlikely to be a lasting differentiator.

Investment and maturity|Match investment to organizational readiness, competitive conditions and risk tolerance; stage commitments around evidence.|Improve data governance before expanding an unproven enterprise rollout.

Responsible AI principles|Fairness, explainability, privacy, security, transparency and robustness should become concrete evaluation and control practices.|Examine errors across relevant groups as well as overall accuracy.

Competing objectives and trade-offs|Document conflicts between business objectives and responsibility requirements, affected parties, decision owners and proportionate controls.|Consider human review before automating a high-impact decision.
Governance by design|Define intended use, data responsibilities, evaluation and oversight during planning and design, before deployment.|Review permitted data use before selecting a dataset.
Human oversight and escalation|Specify when people review, stop or take over an AI process and who has decision authority.|Escalate an important unsupported claim for authorized verification.

Cross-functional governance and accountability|Include business, technical, data and relevant oversight roles with explicit decision responsibilities.|Assign owners for use approval, source maintenance and incident handling.

Compliance risk identification|Determine intended use, data types, jurisdictions and applicable organizational requirements before evaluating compliance risks.|Consult the responsible specialists before reusing personal information.

Access control and data security|Grant only necessary permissions and enforce them in data and tool systems; prompts alone cannot implement reliable access control.|A retrieval assistant must not expose personnel files to unauthorized users.

AI risk classification|Classify a use case by potential impact, affected parties and controls to prioritize oversight.|An internal drafting aid and a consequential automated decision need different controls.

Production monitoring and incidents|Operate logging, quality checks, escalation, fallback and incident response throughout deployment.|Restrict an affected use when error rates rise, then investigate.

Bias across the lifecycle|Sampling, labeling, objectives and deployment context can introduce bias; evaluate relevant subgroup outcomes over time.|A stable average score may hide worsening performance for one group.

Harmful content and intellectual property|Review content risks, input permissions and intended output uses; define review and remediation processes.|Check publication rights and content suitability before releasing generated material.

Hallucination and reliability|A hallucination is plausible but unsupported or incorrect generated content; manage reliability through evidence, evaluation and appropriate review.|Check whether a citation actually supports the claim.

Organizational readiness|Assess leadership alignment, data, culture, infrastructure and governance required to adopt and sustain AI.|A successful demo is insufficient without data owners and operating support.
AI maturity|The stage of organizational capability, from exploration through experiments to repeatable operation at scale.|Running one pilot differs from maintaining several monitored services.
Capability gaps|Identify specific shortfalls in people, processes, technology and governance that prevent intended outcomes.|Replacing a model does not teach employees how to verify its answers.

Roadmaps and investment sequencing|Connect capability building to strategic goals and current readiness through evidence-based milestones.|Establish data ownership and evaluation before expanding the use case.

Data readiness and silos|Assess quality, accessibility and appropriate sharing; disconnected data sources can obstruct consistent use.|Reconcile different customer-field definitions across departments.
Data strategy and ownership|Assign intended uses, accountable owners, quality maintenance and sharing rules.|Name an owner for policy updates and retain versions and access limits.

Infrastructure requirements|Assess compute, storage, networks, integration, monitoring, security and operations against workload needs and cost.|An interactive service also needs acceptable latency and fallback behavior.

Executive support and AI champions|Leaders align goals, resources and accountability; champions support communication and practice within governance.|A business sponsor explains pilot goals and invites employee feedback.
Cross-functional teams|Combine business, technical and oversight capabilities with clear delivery and incident responsibilities.|Know who can pause a risky feature during a pilot.
Transparent communication|Explain timing, expected outcomes, role impacts, support and uncertainties; enable two-way feedback.|Address employees' job concerns rather than only mandating tool use.

Cultural barriers|Distinguish risk aversion, resistance to change and fear of failure; respond with feedback, safe experimentation and support.|Low adoption may reflect poor task fit or trust problems.

Workforce development|Build role-specific AI literacy through practical tasks, training, proofs of concept and responsible use exercises.|Practice verifying citations and escalating uncertain answers.

Changing roles and human strengths|Redesign manual work, oversight and AI collaboration while preserving human judgment, empathy and creativity.|AI drafts a message; a person assesses its context and authorizes sending.
Iterative transformation|Progress through ideation, experimentation, launch and scaling with feedback and decision gates.|Start with a small test and use its results to decide the next step.

From quick wins to scale|Verify an initial result, then test whether data, workflows and support transfer to additional teams.|Volunteer pilot success does not establish suitability for every department.

Center of excellence (CoE)|A shared capability that supports standards, reusable practices and cross-functional collaboration without removing business accountability.|Reuse validated evaluation methods across several teams.
Continuous feedback and value tracking|Monitor use, quality, risks, costs and longer-term outcomes to adapt the transformation plan.|Account creation alone does not demonstrate business value.

Pilot-to-production transition|Establish ownership, operations, governance, support and incident procedures before operating beyond an experiment.|Confirm monitoring, on-call responsibility and rollback before launch.

Enterprise rollout|Assess differences in data, performance, continuity, training and support as adoption expands in controlled stages.|Pause an unsuitable departmental rollout until missing conditions are addressed.
